title: Your consumer is structurally slower than your producer indefinitely — what happens, given Kafka has no built-in backpressure?
shortTitle: Your consumer is structurally slower than your producer indefinitely — what happens, given Kafka has no built-in backpressure?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka decouples producers and consumers through a durable log, so a producer is never slowed down by a slow consumer; there is no end-to-end backpressure that throttles the producer. If a consumer group's aggregate processing rate is permanently below the producer's rate, the gap accumulates as ever-growing consumer lag, which is the number of messages between the latest produced offset and the committed consumer offset. Lag grows without bound, end-to-end latency grows with it, and eventually the oldest unconsumed messages are deleted by retention before the consumer ever reads them, which is silent data loss from the consumer's perspective.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has one clerk opening a mail slot and reading transfer letters, while ten branches keep dropping letters into the slot faster than the clerk can read. The mailbox (the Kafka log) is huge, so the branches never have to wait; they just keep dropping letters. But the pile the clerk has not read keeps growing every single day. Rajesh's transfer letter sinks deeper into the unread pile, so by the time the clerk reaches it, hours have passed. Worse, the mailbox has a rule that letters older than seven days are shredded. If the clerk never catches up, Rajesh's letter is shredded before it is ever read, and nobody is told.
s1_definition.oneliner: With no backpressure, a permanently slow consumer causes lag to grow forever, latency to climb, and eventually retention to delete unread messages — so you must fix the throughput imbalance, not wait for Kafka to slow the producer.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka decouples producers and consumers through a durable log, so a producer is never slowed down by a slow consumer; there is no end-to-end backpressure that throttles the producer. If a consumer group's aggregate processing rate is permanently below the producer's rate, the gap accumulates as ever-growing consumer lag, which is the number of messages between the latest produced offset and the committed consumer offset. Lag grows without bound, end-to-end latency grows with it, and eventually the oldest unconsumed messages are deleted by retention before the consumer ever reads them, which is silent data loss from the consumer's perspective.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has one clerk opening a mail slot and reading transfer letters, while ten branches keep dropping letters into the slot faster than the clerk can read. The mailbox (the Kafka log) is huge, so the branches never have to wait; they just keep dropping letters. But the pile the clerk has not read keeps growing every single day. Rajesh's transfer letter sinks deeper into the unread pile, so by the time the clerk reaches it, hours have passed. Worse, the mailbox has a rule that letters older than seven days are shredded. If the clerk never catches up, Rajesh's letter is shredded before it is ever read, and nobody is told.

**One line to remember:** With no backpressure, a permanently slow consumer causes lag to grow forever, latency to climb, and eventually retention to delete unread messages — so you must fix the throughput imbalance, not wait for Kafka to slow the producer.

sections.s2_technical:
The first thing to internalize is that Kafka deliberately has no end-to-end backpressure. A producer writes to the log and gets acknowledged based only on broker replication; it does not know or care how far behind consumers are. This decoupling is a feature, because it lets producers and consumers scale and fail independently, but it means the system will never automatically slow the producer to match a slow consumer. The consequence of a permanent rate imbalance is unbounded lag.

Lag is a concrete, measurable quantity. For each partition, lag equals the log end offset, which is the offset of the next message to be produced, minus the consumer's committed offset. You read it with the consumer group tool: `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group settlement-apply --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092` shows a LAG column per partition. If the producer rate exceeds the consumer rate indefinitely, this number climbs steadily. Two bad things follow. End-to-end latency, the time from when a message is produced to when it is processed, grows roughly in proportion to lag divided by consumer throughput. And because the log has retention, configured by `retention.ms` or `retention.bytes`, the broker eventually deletes the oldest segments. If lag grows until the committed offset points at data that has already been deleted, the consumer skips forward to the earliest available offset and those messages are lost to it, usually surfacing as an offset-out-of-range situation governed by `auto.offset.reset`.

Now the fixes, because the real answer to the interviewer is how you resolve the imbalance. The most direct lever is consumer parallelism: add consumers to the group up to the number of partitions, because the maximum useful parallelism in a group equals the partition count. If you already have one consumer per partition and still cannot keep up, you must add partitions to the topic so you can add more consumers, accepting the key-remapping caveat that comes with repartitioning. Beyond scaling out, you speed up each consumer: process records in parallel within a consumer using a worker pool while being careful about offset commit ordering, batch expensive operations such as database writes, remove per-record synchronous calls to slow dependencies, and tune `max.poll.records` and `fetch.max.bytes` so each poll does useful bulk work. You can also offload: if each message triggers heavy work, have the consumer quickly hand the work to an internal bounded queue or a separate scaled worker tier, which is how you create application-level backpressure since Kafka gives you none.

Application-level backpressure deserves emphasis because it is the real answer to "Kafka has no backpressure." You build it yourself. A common pattern is the consumer uses `pause()` and `resume()` on partitions when its internal work queue is full, so it stops fetching more until it drains, which prevents it from pulling messages it cannot yet handle and keeps memory bounded. In Spring Kafka you achieve similar control with container concurrency and by not acknowledging until work completes. Reactive frameworks like Reactor Kafka expose real backpressure to the application layer by only requesting as many records as downstream demand allows. None of this slows the producer, but it keeps the consumer stable and makes lag an explicit, managed signal rather than an unbounded memory or latency problem.

Senior-level nuances: first, if the imbalance is only bursty rather than permanent, lag is healthy and self-correcting, and the log is precisely the buffer that absorbs the burst, so do not over-engineer for a steady-state problem you do not have. Second, you must size retention so that it comfortably exceeds your worst-case recovery time, giving you room to catch up after an incident without losing data. Third, you should alert on lag trend, not just absolute lag, because a steadily rising lag is the early warning of a structural imbalance long before retention deletes anything. Fourth, watch out for a single hot partition masquerading as a global throughput problem, because one slow or oversized partition can dominate lag even when the group as a whole has spare capacity.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India ingests card-authorization events into the `card.auth` topic and a consumer group performs a fraud score on each one, which involves a slow model call. Producers emit two thousand events per second during the day. Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) generate card authorizations.

Problem 1 — the fraud scorer processes only one thousand two hundred events per second with its current setup, so it is permanently eight hundred per second behind. Because Kafka never slows the producers, the unprocessed backlog grows all day. This is the no-backpressure reality: lag climbs without bound.

Problem 2 — retention on `card.auth` is six hours. During a heavy day the lag grew to represent more than six hours of events, so the oldest authorizations were deleted before the scorer read them, meaning some fraud checks never happened. This is the silent data loss that retention causes when a slow consumer never catches up.

Our runnable demo simulates a producer rate and a consumer rate over time, tracks lag, shows lag crossing the retention horizon and causing dropped events, and then applies two fixes: scaling consumers up to the partition count, and adding application-level backpressure with a bounded queue and pause/resume so the consumer stays stable. The classes are `BackpressureDemo`, `PartitionedTopic`, `ConsumerGroup`, and `BoundedWorkQueue`.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092,kafka-3:9092
    consumer:
      group-id: fraud-scorer
      enable-auto-commit: false
      max-poll-records: 500          # bulk work per poll
      properties:
        fetch.max.bytes: 10485760
        max.poll.interval.ms: 600000 # allow heavy batches without being kicked
    listener:
      concurrency: 12                # one listener thread per partition (topic has 12)
      ack-mode: manual
# Topic card.auth: retention.ms sized well above worst-case recovery time (e.g. 72h)
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: producers emitting two thousand card authorizations per second, a fraud scorer consuming at one thousand two hundred per second, and a six-hour retention.

Step 1: Every second two thousand events are appended to the log and acknowledged to producers purely on replication. Producers never slow down, regardless of the scorer's state.

Step 2: The scorer processes one thousand two hundred events that second, so eight hundred events accumulate as new lag. Lag rises by eight hundred every second, climbing steadily through the day because the imbalance is structural, not bursty.

Step 3: End-to-end latency rises with lag. A card authorization produced now will not be fraud-scored until the scorer works through everything ahead of it, so Rajesh's authorization might be scored hours after it occurred, which for fraud is effectively useless.

Step 4: Lag eventually represents more than six hours of events. The broker deletes the oldest segments per the retention policy, and those authorizations are gone before the scorer reads them. The scorer's committed offset falls off the start of the log, so it jumps forward and those events are never scored, a silent loss of fraud checks.

Step 5: After scaling the group to process two thousand four hundred per second, each second consumes more than is produced, so lag drains and stabilizes near zero, latency returns to seconds, and nothing is dropped. Separately, the bounded work queue with pause and resume keeps the consumer's memory bounded during spikes by applying the backpressure Kafka itself does not provide.

Final output:

```
[2026-10-24 23:05:33] [INFO] === Before fix: 1 consumer group @ 1200/sec (structurally slow) ===
[2026-10-24 23:05:33] [SEVERE] Final lag=43200000 events; DROPPED by retention=19872000 (fraud checks NEVER ran — silent loss)
[2026-10-24 23:05:33] [INFO] === Fix 1: scale consumers to match (12 partitions, 2400/sec) ===
[2026-10-24 23:05:33] [INFO] Final lag=0 events; nothing dropped, consumer keeps up
[2026-10-24 23:05:33] [INFO] === Fix 2: application backpressure keeps memory bounded ===
[2026-10-24 23:05:33] [INFO] Bounded queue held at capacity 5000 (consumer paused instead of exhausting heap)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka deliberately has no end-to-end backpressure, and that is the key to this question. A producer is acknowledged based only on broker replication and never learns or cares how far behind the consumers are, which is exactly what lets producers and consumers scale and fail independently. The flip side is that if a consumer group's processing rate is permanently below the producer's rate, nothing in Kafka will slow the producer down. Instead the gap accumulates as consumer lag, which is the difference between the latest produced offset and the consumer's committed offset, and that lag grows without bound.

Three bad things follow from unbounded lag. End-to-end latency climbs roughly in proportion to lag over consumer throughput, so a message produced now might be processed hours later, which for something like fraud scoring is worthless. Memory can blow up if the consumer naively keeps fetching messages it cannot process. And most dangerously, retention eventually deletes the oldest unread segments, so if lag grows past the retention horizon, those messages are gone before the consumer ever reads them. The consumer's offset falls off the start of the log and it jumps forward, silently losing data.

On the National Bank of India card-authorization pipeline we lived this. Producers emitted two thousand events per second while the fraud scorer managed only twelve hundred, so lag grew all day and eventually crossed the six-hour retention window, which meant some authorizations were deleted before they were ever fraud-scored. The fix had three parts. First, we scaled consumer parallelism up to the partition count, and because that was still not enough we added partitions so we could add more consumers, so steady-state consumption exceeded production and lag drained to near zero. Second, we made each consumer faster by batching the database writes and parallelizing the slow model call with a worker pool. Third, we built application-level backpressure ourselves, since Kafka gives none, using a bounded internal queue and the consumer's pause and resume so that when the queue fills the consumer stops fetching and keeps its memory bounded instead of collapsing.

The principle I emphasize is that because Kafka will not throttle the producer for you, a structural throughput imbalance is an application design problem you must solve by scaling and speeding up the consumer side and by sizing retention above your worst-case recovery time. I also alert on lag trend rather than just absolute lag, because a steadily rising lag is the early warning of a structural imbalance, and I watch for a single hot partition that can make the whole group look slow even when it has spare capacity. If the imbalance is only bursty, I do nothing special, because the log is precisely the buffer designed to absorb bursts and the lag will self-correct.
